species.name: Atlantic tarpon
specs: Can reach about 8 feet and 300 lb (FWC).
Feeds on fishes and large crustaceans. Adults consume mid-water prey such as mullet, pinfish and marine catfish; crabs are important prey in some seasonal inlet fisheries.

Primarily coastal and inshore as adults, with offshore migrations to spawn. Juveniles commonly occupy estuaries and can use freshwater habitats. The current sources do not establish one universal preferred depth range.

Large, slow-growing coastal migratory fish. Adults concentrate in South Florida during cooler months and are widespread along Florida's coast in summer. Juveniles use estuarine and freshwater nursery habitats; adults migrate offshore to spawn. Tarpon gulp air at the surface and tolerate a wide salinity range.

FWC reports a Florida spawning season of May through September. Florida Museum describes typical spawning in May, June and July and extensive migrations to offshore spawning areas. The Keys spring adult run is a seasonal movement pattern and should not be conflated with the full statewide spawning window.

species.name: Bonefish
specs: Can reach about 3 feet and 15-18 lb, though fish over 10 lb are uncommon. FWC reports typical Florida catches averaging roughly 3-5 lb.
Feeds primarily on benthic invertebrates including shrimp, crabs and other small crustaceans found in seagrass and sand-flat sediments.

Shallow-water flats specialist, often in less than one foot of water over seagrass and sometimes white sand. Small schools move across grass and sand flats searching for shrimp, crabs and other invertebrates. Fish are wary and rely on speed and a deeply forked tail. Northern Florida Keys telemetry also documents use of deeper channels that may provide refuge; this does not locate fish in real time.

Some Bahamas studies document spawning-site linkages and seasonal movements, but those findings should not be assumed for South Florida. FWC reports spawning from November through May, probably in deep or offshore water; the timing and routes of individual South Florida spawning migrations remain incompletely understood.

species.name: Common snook
specs: Up to about 48 inches and 50 lb; Florida state record 45 lb 12 oz (FWC).
Primarily fishes and large crustaceans. FWC lists live pinfish, small mullet, shrimp and sardines among effective baits; diet studies document fishes and crustaceans.

Inshore coastal fish using mangrove shorelines, seagrass beds, beaches, channels, river mouths and other structure. Snook orient into moving water and ambush prey carried by the current. Juveniles use sheltered mangrove-lined swamps, bayous, rivers and creeks; adults use broad estuarine habitat and move between upper-estuary overwintering areas and higher-salinity spawning sites.
Florida spawning generally runs April/May through September/October. Major inlets and coastal river mouths are documented spawning locations. Exact annual timing varies with climate and temperature.

species.name: Hogfish
specs: Can reach about 36 inches; FWC reports a Florida state record of 19 lb 8 oz.
Benthic invertebrates including mollusks, crabs and other small crustaceans. Uses its elongated snout to root through sand and sediment.

Juveniles settle in shallow inshore nursery habitat such as seagrass beds. As they mature, hogfish move toward deeper rocky bottoms, ledges and offshore reefs. The current FWC profile does not establish a single preferred depth band.

Reef-associated wrasse that forages by rooting through sand and sediment, often around reefs, ledges and hard bottom. Adults may associate with gorgonian-rich reef habitat. Juveniles use shallow inshore nursery areas before moving deeper with growth.

Breeding season can extend November-June, peaking around March-April according to FWC. Spawning is typically in late afternoon; do not treat the full breeding window as a precise daily or local aggregation forecast.

Coastal waters near structure. Adults commonly use reefs, ledges and shelf-edge habitat; juveniles use shallower vegetated nursery habitats. The existing 25-95 m depth range is not a universal species depth preference and is retained only as a provisional model screening range.

Adults associate with reefs, ledges, wrecks and other structure; juveniles use shallow seagrass and mangrove habitat. In the Florida Keys, adults make seasonal movements to known spawning aggregation sites, including Riley's Hump in the Dry Tortugas. Aggregation locations are discrete and should not be inferred from generic reef polygons.

FWC's Florida species profile reports spawning in July and August. Florida Keys research documents seasonal spawning migrations and aggregations at discrete sites. Full-moon timing and aggregation behavior are location-specific and should not be treated as a universal calendar for all reefs.

Benthic feeder that roots through sand and seagrass flats for crabs, shrimp, mollusks and other crustaceans; also takes polychaetes, small fishes and other invertebrates.

Uses shallow sandy and seagrass flats and intertidal areas to forage, often moving onto flats with incoming tides from adjacent channels and basins. Smaller fish commonly school; larger adults are more solitary or occur in pairs. Adults also use wrecks and deeper reef structures. Lower Florida Keys telemetry documents use of both shallow flats and deeper Florida Reef Tract habitat, including reef depths around 15–40 m in the study area.

Lower Florida Keys telemetry reported reef occupancy peaking from March through September, especially April-May, and interpreted this pattern as associated with spawning. Treat this as study-area evidence, not a statewide calendar or proof that every reef polygon is spawning habitat.

species.name: Yellowtail snapper
specs: Commonly 2-5 lb; FWC reports a maximum around 30 inches and 5 lb. Florida state record: 8 lb 9 oz.
Adults are commonly associated with offshore reef habitat; NOAA Fisheries and stock-assessment sources describe adult use of roughly 10-70 m, while juveniles use shallower nursery habitats.

A reef-associated schooling snapper, commonly found over or near coral reefs and other hard structure. Adults feed on fishes and invertebrates and often rise into the water column to feed. Juveniles use seagrass, mangroves and back-reef nursery habitat.
FWC describes spawning in mid-summer; regional fisheries sources report a broader April-August spawning period in the southeastern United States.
NOAA Fisheries reports a typical lifespan of 6-14 years, with older individuals documented.

A separate study reported critical thermal maxima of 36.4 ± 0.5 and 37.9 ± 0.5 °C and habitat temperatures up to 40.6 °C. spots.title: Government Cut (inlet)

factor_diagnostics.value_notes: Partly sourced for broad occurrence and a regional bottom-temperature association, not for a locally calibrated SST suitability curve. A 1967–1969 offshore Mississippi study recorded 6,457 spot, observed specimens at bottom temperatures of about 14.1–29.5°C, and reported greatest apparent temperature preference/catch association around 19.0–21.9°C. This is useful evidence that overlaps the configured 16–26°C ideal interval, but it is old, offshore, Mississippi-specific, and based on bottom rather than surface temperature. NOAA's southeastern U.S. coastal survey and the Florida Museum collection profile document a broader Florida distribution, including South Florida, while USGS/FishBase summaries repeat an older statement that spot are absent from southern Florida. spots.title: Hillsboro Inlet (inlet)

factor_diagnostics.value_notes: Partly sourced for broad occurrence and a regional bottom-temperature association, not for a locally calibrated SST suitability curve. A 1967–1969 offshore Mississippi study recorded 6,457 spot, observed specimens at bottom temperatures of about 14.1–29.5°C, and reported greatest apparent temperature preference/catch association around 19.0–21.9°C. This is useful evidence that overlaps the configured 16–26°C ideal interval, but it is old, offshore, Mississippi-specific, and based on bottom rather than surface temperature. NOAA's southeastern U.S. coastal survey and the Florida Museum collection profile document a broader Florida distribution, including South Florida, while USGS/FishBase summaries repeat an older statement that spot are absent from southern Florida. Treat southern Florida site applicability as uncertain and verify local occurrence before relying on this factor.

factor_diagnostics.value_notes: Keys tagging (FWC and FIU): most adults arrived in April once water reached 26 C and left in June at 27-29 C, with peak presence in May (26-28 C). The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's 1978 Mid-Atlantic Bight atlas records adult white grunt at 15–33.6°C, with occasional records in 35°C water but notes fish do not remain long at that extreme; it also describes Florida reef/flat habitat at roughly 6–24 m. This is a broad recorded occurrence range, not a preferred SST band. FishBase reports a model-derived preferred-temperature estimate of 23.4–28°C (mean 25.9°C; 342 spatial cells), which overlaps the configured 22–29°C ideal interval, but it is a distribution/model association rather than a controlled physiological preference or local South Florida catch-response curve. Ambient temperature ranged 8.7-23.6 °C (mean 15.2 °C); 52% of time was 13-16 °C, with a peak around 14 °C, and 95% of surface-oriented records occurred at 12-19 °C. This supports thermal relevance, but ambient temperature at fish depth is not always satellite SST; the configured 14-22 °C range and 16-20 °C ideal are shifted warmer than the central observed temperatures.
